title: VPC isolation patterns, endpoints & DNS handoff - POC workshop notes
content:
Context:
This doc captures notes from the 2024-11-04 workshop with Customer X (regulated fintech) where we sketched VPC isolation patterns for an initial POC. Goal for the POC: prove private network connectivity between customer workloads (in their VPC) and Redwood Private runtime without exposing plaintext inference traffic to public internet, while preserving observability and meeting their compliance controls (e.g., allowlist egress destinations, flow logs retained for 90 days).

High-level POC constraints and non-negotiables:
- Customer requires no public internet egress for inference traffic (no NATing to public endpoints).
- Must support mutual TLS between customer service and Redwood Private control plane endpoints.
- Minimal change to customer infra (prefer configuration vs. new infra).
- Support for split-DNS: internal hostnames resolve to private endpoints inside customer network.
- Auditability: VPC flow logs + centralized metadata for requests.

Primary design goals for evaluation:
1) Isolation: traffic to model endpoints stays on private connectivity path.
2) Operability: ability for SEs and customer's cloud/security teams to debug connectivity failures.
3) Incremental rollout: start with one model (gpt-embedding-8k) and scale.
4) Fallback: graceful failover to hosted API if private path unavailable (policy-driven).

Options considered (short list + pros/cons):
A) Shared Transit Hub (TGW / Hub-and-spoke) with VPC attachments
   - Pros: centralized routing, easiest to add multiple accounts/VPCs, supports route-based firewalls and inspection appliances.
   - Cons: Requires customer to accept TGW attachments and cross-account permissions; potentially slow to provision; adds single hub failure surface we must account for.

B) VPC Peering + Proxy/Relay in customer VPC (sidecar or NAT instance replacement)
   - Pros: Simple L2-like connectivity, no transit gateway costs, no central hub to manage.
   - Cons: Peering doesn't support transitive routing; for multiple spokes this becomes N^2. Also private DNS handoff needs conditional forwarders or host entries.

C) PrivateLink / Interface Endpoint (AWS) or Private Service Connect (GCP) — platform-hosted endpoint facing customer account
   - Pros: Lowest blast radius for customer, AWS PrivateLink keeps traffic private and controlled; no route table changes in customer VPC.
   - Cons: Requires provisioning interface endpoints and ENIs; cross-account endpoint costs and ENI limits; DNS configuration needed for hostnames to resolve to endpoint IPs.

D) VPN / Direct Connect with BGP + route filters (more common for regulated environments)
   - Pros: Meets strict compliance, full network isolation, supports on-prem customers.
   - Cons: Lead time (days-weeks), operational overhead, costs.

Our recommended path for the POC (consensus): Hybrid approach — PrivateLink-style interface endpoints (C) for control-plane & telemetry + a small managed relay in customer VPC (B) to handle large-burst inference egress and caching. Rationale:
- PrivateLink handles control plane and auth without touching internet; minimal route changes; customer security team happy with endpoint model.
- Local relay (lightweight, autoscaling EC2 or Fargate service) gives the customer visibility into outbound inference streams, lets them insert WAF/inspection, and avoids creating a large number of endpoint ENIs for each model variant.

Architecture sketch (ASCII):
Customer Account VPC A (private)                        Redwood Private VPC
+-------------------------------+                       +-------------------+
| Customer services (app)       | <--interface endpoint-> | PrivateLink ENI    |
|  - sidecar/egress-relay (Fargate) - forwards ->--------| (control-plane)    |
|  - security appliance (optional) |                     | Redwood runtime   |
+-------------------------------+                       +-------------------+
DNS: customer resolver -> conditional forward to PrivateLink DNS; fallback to public resolver for non-internal names.

DNS strategies (detailed):
1) Conditional forwarder / Resolver rules (AWS Route 53 Resolver rules or GCP Cloud DNS forwarding):
   - For hostnames under *.redwood-private.internal -> forward to Redwood Resolver (via inbound Resolver endpoints or PrivateLink DNS/IP).
   - For health-check hostnames, forward to public to allow external monitoring as needed.
2) Split-horizon DNS: customer maintains internal zone with records pointing to ENI IPs for critical endpoints.
3) Host-based override (short-term during POC): update /etc/hosts or sidecar env var to point service clients at the relay IP. Fast but not scalable.

Endpoint choices and lifecycle for POC:
- Control plane: PrivateLink interface endpoint (tls + mTLS). Customers accept CA cert and mTLS client certs per service account.
- Data plane (large token streams): local relay that uses VPC peering back to Redwood Private compute plane or uses private egress to Redwood peering connection.
- Option to test direct VPC peering for a single customer proof of concept to compare latency/cost vs relay path.

Egress controls and guardrails:
- Customer-side: ACLs and security groups restricting relay egress to Redwood IP ranges/subnets only; egress proxy enforces allowlist of domain names (SNI inspection) and TLS inspection if required.
- Redwood-side: accept connections only from customer-assigned source subnets/endpoint ENIs and validate TLS client certs.
- Flow logging: enable VPC Flow Logs -> central S3/logs account; ship to Splunk/Datadog with 90-day retention.

Observability and debugging plan:
- Connectivity test script (separate artifact): performs DNS resolution, TLS handshake check, simple POST of a test prompt and asserts response.
- Metrics to capture in POC: TLS handshake success rate, P99 RTT for first token, total tokens/sec, connection churn rate.
- Recommended temporary debug features: tcpdump on relay (rotated), enable ENI-level packet mirroring when needed, and capture mTLS handshakes on both sides for correlation.

Operational runbook (POC scope):
1) Pre-workshop checklist (SE + customer infra team): share a short runbook and required IAM statements for PrivateLink creation.
2) Customer creates a new VPC/segment for POC (keeps isolation); provide subnet CIDRs and AZ mapping.
3) Redwood provisions PrivateLink service and shares service name.
4) Customer creates Interface Endpoint and (optional) Resolver rules; attach security groups.
5) Deploy relay (Fargate) inside customer's POC VPC; test connectivity to PrivateLink control-plane.
6) Swap a single test service to route requests via relay; run perf/latency tests.
7) Collect logs and evaluate compliance checklist.

POC success criteria (agreed):
- 100% of inference traffic for test workloads flows over private connectivity (no public egress observed).
- Latency meets SLO: tail <= 2x hosted API baseline for 95% of requests.
- Observability: flow logs + telemetry available and ingested into customer SIEM.
- Security: mTLS handshake validated and documented key rotation process.

Unresolved questions / next actions:
- Q: Are we allowed to provision an ENI in customer VPC on their behalf or must the customer create endpoint? (Assumption: customer will create endpoint; ask security team to confirm.)
- Q: Does the customer require full TLS inspection for inference payloads? If yes, discuss legal/PII implications.
- Action: SEs to provide a minimized IAM JSON for endpoint creation and an example Resolver rule (assigned to Connor).
- Action: Run a small bench: compare relay vs direct peering for P99 token latency (assigned to Marco).

Appendix: quick checklist for workshop demo
- Have a pre-baked CloudFormation/Terraform snippet to create: VPC, subnet, SecurityGroup, Route53 Resolver rules (if AWS).
- Demo script: DNS resolve -> TLS handshake -> POST prompt -> show tokens streaming -> show flow logs appearing in Splunk.
- Fallback test: simulate endpoint failure and show automatic switch to hosted API (verify fallback policy).

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep relay lightweight (stateless) and avoid caching sensitive customer data by default. Provide an opt-in cache config.
- Consider offering an ephemeral test PrivateLink service to accelerate POC onboarding (ask infra about quota/cost implications).
- Document cert rotation cadence and automation (ACME not usable for internal mTLS).

References and links:
- Internal SE checklist: SE-POC-templates/privatelink-snippets
- Jira: SE-4321 (POC tracking)
- Related infra PR: github.com/redwood/infra#779

End of notes.
